items.title: Accountability and the Seven Principles
items.source: Committee on Standards in Public Life, The Seven Principles of Public Life; Cabinet Office, project delivery guidance
items.body: The Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) is the individual accountable for the success of a project or programme and for achieving its outcomes. In a department, the accounting officer, usually the permanent secretary, is accountable to Parliament for how the whole organisation spends public money. Everyone who holds public office is expected to follow the Seven Principles of Public Life: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership. In practice that means declaring interests, being careful with gifts and hospitality, making decisions on evidence and being willing to explain them to the public.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for the success of a major project?
Who is usually the accounting officer of a government department?
Which list gives the Seven Principles of Public Life?

options.text: Speed, thrift, secrecy, loyalty, profit, privacy, popularity
Equality, liberty, fraternity, thrift, order, justice, growth
Selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership
Planning, delivery, risk, finance, audit, law, data

questions.prompt: A supplier offers the SRO of a programme tickets to a sporting event while a contract extension is being decided. What should happen?
questions.answer: Decline the offer, or at minimum declare it and have it recorded in the gifts and hospitality register. The offer is made at a time that could look like influence, so integrity and objectivity are at risk. Tell the line manager or ethics contact, consider the conflict and keep the decision-making visible.
questions.rubric: Should say to decline or declare, record in the register, recognise the perceived influence, apply Nolan principles of integrity and objectivity, and escalate if needed.

items.title: Boards, delegation and decision records
items.source: Cabinet Office, project delivery guidance; local authority constitutions
items.body: A programme board oversees the work, makes the key decisions that are beyond the delivery team and resolves escalations. A scheme of delegation sets out who can take which decisions up to what value and in what circumstances, so everyone knows who may commit money or approve changes. Decisions are recorded with the options considered, the reasons and who agreed, so they can be explained, scrutinised and defended later. Risks and issues escalate along a defined route: team, programme, board, sponsor, with time limits and thresholds. A route that nobody has agreed in advance fails when it is most needed.

questions.prompt: What does a programme board do?

options.text: Oversees the work, makes the key decisions and resolves escalations

questions.prompt: What does a scheme of delegation set out?

options.text: Who can take which decisions, up to what value and in what circumstances

questions.prompt: Why record the reasons for a decision as well as the decision itself?

options.text: So the decision can be explained, scrutinised and defended later

questions.prompt: Design an escalation route for a programme risk and say what makes it work.
questions.answer: Set thresholds for when a risk moves up (team, programme manager, board, sponsor), name an owner at each level and a time limit for a response, record the escalation and the decision, and test the route with a real example. It works when everyone knows it in advance and it is used without blame.
questions.rubric: Should include tiers, thresholds, owners, time limits, recording, and it being agreed and understood in advance.

items.title: Approvals and briefing decision makers
items.source: Cabinet Office guidance on writing for Ministers; Local Government Act 2000
items.body: Papers for a cabinet, committee or ministerial decision should lead with the decision needed, then give the options considered, the evidence, the financial and legal implications, the risks and a recommendation. A decision maker should be able to read the first page and know what they are being asked to decide. In English councils, significant decisions by the executive are listed in a forward plan published in advance, so that members and the public know what is coming and can take part. If a serious legal or financial risk comes to light late, it must be raised at once and included in the paper rather than left out; the decision may need to be delayed.

questions.prompt: What should a decision paper do first?

options.text: Give the full history of the project
Hide the risks until the end

questions.prompt: What should a briefing for a minister or member contain?

options.text: The decision, the options, the evidence, the risks and a recommendation

questions.prompt: Why do councils publish a forward plan of key decisions?

options.text: So members and the public know what decisions are coming and can take part
To decide who is invited to lunch

questions.prompt: The committee paper is due tomorrow. Legal has just told you the proposal carries a significant risk of challenge. What do you do?
questions.answer: Raise it immediately with the sponsor and the report author, include the risk and the legal advice in the paper in plain terms, and recommend any change or delay needed. Do not leave it out or soften it to meet the deadline; decision makers need to know the risk to decide.
questions.rubric: Should say raise at once, include in the paper, be transparent, recommend mitigation or delay, and not hide the risk to meet a deadline.

items.title: Strategic review and closing a service
items.source: Cabinet Office, project delivery guidance; HM Treasury, Green Book
items.body: A strategic review asks whether the service is still needed, whether it is meeting its outcomes and whether it is still the best use of money. The options are to continue as is, change it, merge it with another service or stop it. If the decision is to stop, a closure plan sets out the steps: legal duties, communication to the public and staff, support for users who need another service, notice on contracts, staff consultation, records and data, assets, and a final report. A closure report records what was achieved, what was spent, what was learned and what risks remain, and it is shared with the board and those who will plan similar work.

questions.prompt: What does a strategic review of a service ask?

options.text: Whether the service is still needed and is meeting its outcomes
Who should be the next leader
What colour the logo should be

questions.prompt: Which is one of the options at a strategic review?

options.text: Continue, change, merge or stop the service
Hand it to the press office

questions.prompt: What should a closure report record?

options.text: What was achieved, what was spent, lessons learned and remaining risks

questions.prompt: Ministers decide to stop a service used by 12,000 people, with two months' notice. What does your closure plan need to cover?
questions.answer: Legal duties and any consultation or equality assessment needed; clear communication to users and staff; support for users to move to alternatives; notice on contracts; staff consultation and redeployment; handling of records and data; assets; a closure report. Check whether the timescale is realistic and escalate if it is not.
questions.rubric: Should cover legal/equality duties, communication, user transition, contract notice, staff, records/data, assets, closure report, and realistic timescale/escalation.
